To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) patient awareness is low, but higher among patients with diabetes and hypertension, and lower among those who are younger, female, or non-white; (2) provider awareness is higher than patient awareness, but varies by provider characteristics; (3) CKD patient awareness is not associated with increased utilization of preventive health services or improved clinical outcomes; and (4) CKD patient and provider awareness is associated with increased knowledge and self-reported adherence to CKD guidelines, respectively.

1) CKD awareness among patients and providers remains unacceptably low, 2) CKD awareness is associated with patient sociodemographic characteristics and health literacy, 3) CKD awareness in providers is associated with provider sociodemographic characteristics, 4) CKD awareness does not appear to be associated with improved clinical outcomes, 5) CKD awareness appears to be associated with increased patient knowledge and patient self-efficacy regarding CKD management.
CKD awareness among patients and providers is low and that more research is needed to determine how to best raise awareness and to determine whether awareness leads to improved clinical outcomes.
